# Week 3: CFA, estimation and fit {.unnumbered}

::: {.week-meta}
Core reading
: @byrne2016, chapter 3, from the hypothesised model to the model as a whole, pp. 69–101 (about 2 hours)

Data
: [Student Life Survey](../course/dataset.qmd), clean file: all 23 items

App
: Fit index explorer

Task style
: Worked example: reproduce, then change one thing and predict the result

:::

## By the end of this week you can

- Explain in outline what maximum-likelihood estimation does.
- Interpret χ², RMSEA with its confidence interval, CFI and TLI.
- Explain why χ² is sensitive to sample size.
- Describe a model's fit without treating cut-offs as pass marks.

## Warm-up

Answer from memory at the start of the session. It takes two minutes and makes earlier ideas easier to recall later.

1. Both scales have a reliability of .80. How much is their correlation weakened? (Week 0)
2. What does fixing a loading to 1 do?

<details class="answers">
<summary>Check your answers</summary>

1. It is multiplied by √(.80 × .80) = .80, so a true correlation of −.60 is observed as about −.48.
2. It sets the latent variable's scale to that of the item.

</details>

## This week in brief

Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) tests a specified measurement model: which items load on which factors. Maximum likelihood finds the parameter values that make the model-implied covariance matrix as close as possible to the observed one. Fit indices summarise how close it is; none of them is a pass mark.

## In the session

- How ML estimation works, in outline.
- The χ² test and why it is sensitive to sample size, with the app.
- RMSEA (with its confidence interval and PCLOSE), CFI and TLI: what each measures and its weaknesses.

## After the session

Read the core reading with these questions in mind, and note your answers in your log:

- Which parameters does Byrne fix, and why is each one fixed rather than estimated?
- What does each fit statistic (χ², RMSEA, CFI and the others she reports) tell her about the model as a whole?
- Why does she not stop at the χ² test?

Read the hypothesised model and the model evaluation closely. Pages that walk through drawing in Amos Graphics repeat Week 2 and can be skimmed.

## Your task this week

1. Reproduce Byrne's chapter 3 model and find each fit index she reports.
2. Specify a five-factor CFA for the Student Life Survey: each scale's items load on their own factor (use `WB5r` for the fifth wellbeing item); all factors correlate.
3. **Predict first:** with N = 520, will the χ² test be significant?
4. Run it and report χ², df, p, RMSEA (90% CI), CFI and TLI. Enter the values, including the independence model's χ² and df, in the fit index explorer and check they match.

## For your SEM log

Write your answers in your log first; then compare.

1. Why is χ² almost always significant in large samples?
2. What does the RMSEA confidence interval add to the point estimate?
3. How would you describe the fit of your Student Life CFA?

<details class="answers model">
<summary>Compare with model answers (after writing your own)</summary>

1. χ² = (N − 1) × the minimum discrepancy. Any model is slightly wrong, and with many cases even a tiny discrepancy produces a large χ².
2. Precision. A narrow interval below .05 is strong evidence of close fit; a wide interval (small df or N) means the data cannot say much.
3. Something like: "χ² was significant, as expected with N = 520, but RMSEA (with its 90% CI) and CFI indicated close fit." Report the values, cite benchmarks as guides (Hu & Bentler, 1999) with their limits (Marsh et al., 2004), and look at local fit next week.

</details>

## Extra resources

Optional. Each is labelled with when it is worth reading.

- **If the fit indices are still unclear:** Kenny's page on [measuring model fit](https://davidakenny.net/cm/fit.htm), about 30 minutes.
- **The source of the usual cut-offs:** @hu1999, abstract and discussion only.
- **Why not to treat them as rules:** @marsh2004.
- **A summary of the indices:** [StatWiki: CFA model fit](https://statwiki.gaskination.com/index.php?title=CFA).
- **Planning sample size:** Preacher and Coffman's [RMSEA power calculator](https://www.quantpsy.org/rmsea/rmsea.htm).
